analysis.one_liner: Strips Social Security numbers and paid medical debt from credit reports and shields fraud victims' files.
analysis.headline: The House never voted on the bill, which would have banned Social Security numbers from credit reports, removed medical debt paid more than a year earlier, and erased court-determined fraud records from credit files.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten the rules for credit reporting agencies. It would ban Social Security numbers from credit reports, require federal cybersecurity exams of the big credit bureaus, and stop the bureaus from reporting medical debt once it has been paid for over a year. It would also keep courts' findings of predatory mortgage lending, domestic financial abuse, and private student loan fraud off consumers' credit files, and give the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau a public list of credit reporting agencies and a study of non-traditional credit data. The House referred it to the Financial Services Committee, which took no action before that Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers whose credit files carry baggage that doesn't reflect their own behavior: people whose paid medical debt dings their score for years, victims of domestic financial abuse whose abusers wrecked their credit, borrowers defrauded by private student lenders, and homeowners stuck with the fallout of court-determined predatory mortgage lending. Consumers also gain a layer of protection against identity theft, since the bureaus could no longer print Social Security numbers in reports or use them to verify identity, and against data breaches, since the CFPB could supervise the big bureaus' cybersecurity. On the other side, the bill would slow down security freezes: placing one by phone or online would take up to 3 business days instead of 1, and lifting one would take up to 3 days instead of 1 hour, so consumers rushing to apply for a mortgage or a loan would wait longer.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers with medical debt or fraud-tainted credit files

how_it_helps.text: Bans large credit reporting agencies from putting Social Security numbers in credit reports or using them to verify a consumer's identity, cutting off a common path for identity theft.
Stops credit reporting agencies from reporting medically necessary debt once it has been paid for more than a year, so a settled medical bill stops dragging down a credit score.

Keeps adverse items off credit reports when a court has found the consumer was a victim of financial abuse by a spouse, family member, or caregiver, of predatory or fraudulent mortgage lending by a financial institution, or of fraud in a private student loan.

Puts the big credit bureaus under Consumer Financial Protection Bureau cybersecurity supervision and examination, and requires the Bureau to publish a public list of credit reporting agencies and study how non-traditional data is used in credit scoring.
Requires credit reports that include public-record information (like court records) to identify the source of that data, so consumers can find and dispute errors.

analysis.who_pays: The credit reporting agencies lose data they currently sell and report — paid medical debt over a year old, and adverse items tied to court findings of fraud or abuse — and would face compliance costs plus CFPB cybersecurity exams. Medical debt collectors lose the reporting lever they use to push people to pay. Consumers pay a small convenience cost: security freezes would take longer to place and much longer to lift. Some of the fraud protections also only trigger after the consumer wins a lawsuit on their own (not a class action), which many people cannot afford to do.
analysis.who_pays_short: Credit bureaus and medical debt collectors

drawbacks.text: The bill lengthens security-freeze timelines: placing a freeze by phone or electronically would go from 1 business day to 3, and lifting one would go from 1 hour to 3 days — a real delay for a consumer trying to unfreeze their credit quickly for a loan or apartment application.

The protections for financially abused consumers, defrauded student borrowers, and predatory-lending victims only apply after a court of competent jurisdiction — in a non-class-action lawsuit — has ruled in the consumer's favor, a bar most ordinary consumers cannot clear without a lawyer.
The medical debt fix is narrow: it only covers debt that has already been paid for more than a year, so unpaid medical bills and recently paid bills would still appear on credit reports.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On balance a genuine, if modest, win for consumers: the Social Security number ban and the paid-medical-debt fix would help a lot of people at real cost to the credit bureaus and collectors. The bill's weaknesses are its reliance on individual lawsuits as the trigger for fraud protections, its narrow one-year window on medical debt, and the slower freeze timelines, which hand a small convenience cost back to consumers. It is a carefully tailored bill, not a sweeping overhaul of the credit reporting system.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it died when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Patrick McHenry, the top Republican on the House Financial Services Committee, introduced the bill on July 18, 2019; it was referred to that committee the same day.
One House Democrat cosponsored the bill. That was the end of its support: the committee held no markup and reported nothing, and no floor vote ever happened.
The 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, and the bill expired with it.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit reporting agencies and medical debt collectors are better off: none of the new limits on what they can report, sell, or be examined for ever took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Credit bureaus and medical debt collectors

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever recorded; the bill's only support came from its Republican sponsor and a single Democratic cosponsor before it died in committee.

industries.note: The bill bans Social Security numbers from their reports, subjects the largest bureaus to CFPB cybersecurity exams, and strips paid medical debt and court-determined fraud items from the files they sell to lenders. Each change cuts data they currently sell and adds compliance burden.
Reporting a paid medical bill is a chief lever for pressuring consumers to pay; barring reports on medically necessary debt paid more than a year earlier removes that lever for older bills.
Defaults tied to court-determined fraud in a private student loan could no longer be reported, weakening the credit-file consequences lenders rely on.

Foreclosures, short sales, and delinquencies tied to court-determined or settlement-covered predatory or fraudulent lending practices could no longer appear on consumers' reports, reducing the industry's collection and deterrent tools in those cases.
